questions.prompt: 25 runs, mean 100, SD 15. Using t(24)~2.064 for the 95% CI, half-width? (2 decimals)
You want to halve the CI half-width of a mean. By what factor must n increase?
A: mean 90, B: mean 84, both SD 10, n=10 each. Cohen's d? (2 decimals)
With n=20000 per group, d=0.03 and p=0.001. What is the right summary?
options: Statistically significant, but the effect is practically negligible.
A large and important effect, since the p-value is so small.
No effect, because the difference of 0.03 is far below the noise.
The test is invalid, because the sample size is much too large.
questions.explanation: Large n makes tiny effects significant.

questions.prompt: With n=4 per group, d=1.2 and p=0.15. What is the right summary?
options: A significant effect, since d is large and p is small enough.
Proof that there is no effect, because p is greater than 0.05.
A negative effect, since the group difference is not significant.
Inconclusive: a possibly large effect measured too imprecisely.
questions.explanation: Absence of significance is not evidence of absence.

questions.prompt: 20 independent tests, alpha=0.05. Bonferroni per-test level? (4 decimals)
50 independent tests at alpha=0.05 with no real effects. Expected number of false positives?
Welch SE for A (s=2, n=4) and B (s=2, n=4)? (3 decimals)
Which is the correct way to combine the uncertainty of two independent group means?
options: Add the standard errors of the two group means directly.
Multiply the standard errors, then take the square root.
Average the standard deviations of the two groups, then divide by n.
Add the variances of the means, then take the square root.

questions.prompt: You run the same seeds for two methods (seed s used in both). Which analysis is more appropriate?
options: Only compare the best seed.
Welch's test treating all runs as independent.
A paired analysis of per-seed differences.
Bonferroni correction.
questions.explanation: Shared seeds pair the runs and reduce variance.

questions.prompt: After seeing the data you switch from a t-test to a one-sided test because it gives p<0.05. What is the problem?
options: There is no problem, because a one-sided test uses the same data.
The test was chosen after seeing the data, which inflates false positives.
One-sided tests are never valid in any experiment, however planned.
t-tests cannot be one-sided, so the new test is a different method.

questions.prompt: Two policies differ by 2.0 points (95% CI -1.0 to 5.0) with six seeds each. Write an honest one-paragraph conclusion and say what you would do next.
rubric: States the estimate and interval and that zero is plausible; avoids claiming a difference or no difference.
Notes the small sample and effect-size uncertainty.
Proposes more seeds computed from the target effect or a paired design.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Explain why a permutation test and a t-test can disagree at n=6 per group, and which you would trust more.
rubric: Permutation is exact under exchangeability; t depends on normality of the means.
With tiny n the t approximation can be off, so p values differ.
Suggests checking both and reporting the interval.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
